Fourth, the EPA proposes changes to certain requirements finalized in March 2024 related to control devices and to provide owners and operators the option to conduct optical gas imaging surveys according to Appendix K for gas processing facilities. Lastly, the EPA proposes changes to correct inadvertent errors and to clarify regulatory language.

SUMMARY: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing 
amendments to the New Source Performance Standards and Emission 
Guidelines for the Crude Oil and Natural Gas Source Category to address 
additional concerns raised with prior regulatory amendments finalized 
in March 2024. Specifically, the EPA is proposing changes in response 
to certain petitions for reconsideration of the March 2024 amendments, 
changes based on policy decisions and supporting legal interpretations, 
and changes that correct and clarify the regulatory text of the new 
source performance standards and emission guidelines. First, the EPA 
proposes to rescind the Super Emitter Program. Second, the EPA proposes 
to subcategorize different types of well sites affected and designated 
facilities to address issues related to the requirements finalized in 
March 2024 for marginal well sites and conventional well sites. Third, 
the EPA proposes changes to address issues related to liquids 
unloading, process controllers, pumps, fugitive emissions, storage 
vessels, covers and closed vent systems, equipment leaks at gas plants, 
and associated gas. Fourth, the EPA proposes changes to certain 
requirements finalized in March 2024 related to control devices and to 
provide owners and operators the option to conduct optical gas imaging 
surveys according to Appendix K for gas processing facilities. Lastly, 
the EPA proposes changes to correct inadvertent errors and to clarify 
regulatory language.

I. Executive Summary

    On March 8, 2024, the EPA published a final rule amending and 
expanding requirements for the Crude Oil and Natural Gas source 
category under Clean Air Act (CAA) sections 111(b) and (d) (``March 
2024 Final Rule'').\1\ The EPA finalized new source performance 
standards (NSPS) for greenhouse gas (GHG) and volatile organic compound 
(VOC) emissions from new, modified, and reconstructed sources in this 
source category, codified in 40 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) part 
60, subpart OOOOb (NSPS OOOOb). The EPA also finalized emission 
guidelines (EG) for GHG emissions from existing sources in this source 
category, codified in 40 CFR part 60, subpart OOOOc (EG OOOOc). The 
NSPS OOOOb applies to thousands of new sources, whose construction, 
reconstruction, or modification began after December 6, 2022, and the 
EG OOOOc covers hundreds of thousands of existing sources in the Crude 
Oil and Natural Gas source category. Crude oil production applicability 
includes the well and extends to the point of custody transfer to the 
crude oil transmission pipeline or any other forms of transportation. 
Natural gas production applicability includes production, processing, 
transmission, and storage, which includes the well and extends to, but 
does not include, the local distribution company custody transfer 
station.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \1\ 89 FR 16820 (March 8, 2024).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The March 2024 Final Rule broke new ground in multiple respects. In 
EG OOOOc, the EPA required States to regulate GHG emissions from 
hundreds of thousands of existing sources in the Crude Oil and Natural 
Gas source category for the first time. This novel and massive task is 
presenting additional and, at times, unforeseen coordination and 
compliance difficulties. For several aspects of NSPS OOOOb and EG 
OOOOc, the EPA promulgated ambitious ``zero-emission requirements'' 
predicated on very different best system of emissions reduction (BSER) 
determinations. With respect to associated gas produced during oil 
extraction, for example, the EPA predicated its zero-emission standard 
for new sources on a BSER of routing gas to sales lines based on the 
assumption that sources would be located in an area where such 
infrastructure--generally owned and operated by third parties--is, or 
would be, established at sufficient scale. Recognizing that not all 
existing sources fit within that assumption, the Agency built 
subcategories into the BSER analysis and resulting presumptive 
standards that allow continued flaring under certain circumstances. For 
new sources, the Agency concluded that it was appropriate to require 
routing to a sales line based, among other things, on a cost-
effectiveness analysis that assumed new sources would be located within 
50 miles of existing infrastructure. This approach broadened the BSER 
analysis from source-centered compliance to one that very heavily 
relied on industry-wide participants unregulated by NSPS OOOOb and EG 
OOOOc, which raised novel legal and policy questions that the Agency 
did not fully grapple with at the time of promulgation. The resulting 
new source standard in the March 2024 Final Rule, as discussed herein, 
risks limiting the development of new oil and gas extraction areas 
where potential sources must hold back until or unless necessary 
infrastructure develops, thereby coming into tension with the economics 
of the industry, national security and energy priorities, and CAA 
section 111's instruction to develop new source standards that can be 
achieved across the Nation.
    After publication of the March 2024 Final Rule, the EPA received 
multiple petitions for reconsideration.\2\ On May 6, 2024, the EPA 
notified certain petitioners and the public that the Agency granted 
reconsideration on two discrete aspects of the March 2024 Final

[[Page 68237]]

Rule: the temporary flaring provisions for associated gas in certain 
situations; and the vent gas net heating value (NHV) continuous 
monitoring requirements and alternative performance test (sampling 
demonstration) option for flares and enclosed combustion 
devices.

associated gas in certain situations; technical changes to the vent gas 
NHV continuous monitoring requirements and alternative performance test 
(sampling demonstration) option for flares and enclosed combustion 
devices).

    On July 31, 2025, the EPA promulgated an interim final rule (``July 
2025 IFR'') which extended deadlines for certain provisions in the NSPS 
OOOOb related to control devices, equipment leaks, storage vessels, 
process controllers, and covers and closed vent systems (CVS) to 
address legitimate concerns, raised by stakeholders, that certain 
regulatory provisions were not currently workable or contained 
problematic regulatory language that frustrates compliance.\12\ Within 
that IFR, the EPA also extended the date for future implementation of 
the Super Emitter Program and extended the State plan submittal 
deadline in EG OOOOc. The EPA solicited public comment on the 
extensions included in the July 2025 IFR. The EPA considered the 
comments received, and then, in December 2025, the EPA promulgated a 
final rule which responded to the comments and reaffirmed the 
conclusions and the regulatory amendments made in the IFR (``December 
2025 Final Rule'').\13\ In response to comments received on the July 
2025 IFR, the December 2025 Final Rule provided an additional 180-day 
extension (from the final rule's effective date) (until June 1, 2026) 
to the compliance dates related to NHV monitoring of flares and 
enclosed combustion devices (ECDs) found in 40 CFR 60.5417b(d)(8)(i) 
through (iv) and (vi), as well as 360 days from the effective date of 
the December 2025 Final Rule (November 30, 2026) for owners and 
operators to submit initial annual reports pursuant to 40 CFR 
60.5420(b).\14\

    This proposal reflects the EPA's reconsideration of additional 
aspects of the March 2024 Final Rule, including some of the Agency's 
prior BSER determinations and the legal and policy positions taken in 
finalizing those determinations. Upon further review, and in light of 
information considered since promulgation, the EPA no longer believes 
that some of the ``zero-emission'' requirements in NSPS OOOOb and EG 
OOOOc are predicated on acceptable assessments of emissions reductions, 
cost effectiveness, and achievability. In some cases, the March 2024 
Final Rule moved from requirements that control 95 percent of emissions 
to standards stated as ``zero-emission'' requirements. However, 
achievability limitations and compliance difficulties, including those 
the EPA anticipated at the time by building in exemptions and those the 
Agency did not foresee, suggest that the requirements' emission 
reductions potential are more modest than previously anticipated. At 
the same time, the Agency very likely underestimated costs because the 
actual costs of compliance are likely higher than the EPA anticipated 
in the March 2024 Final Rule. The resulting reconsideration--taking 
into account more modest emissions reductions and more significant 
costs--suggests that significant aspects of some BSER determinations 
and resulting standards in the March 2024 Final Rule are inappropriate. 
EPA solicits comment on further considerations relative to the March 
2024 Final Rule, such as those petitioners have flagged.
    In this action, the EPA proposes the following:

 Rescinding the Super Emitter Program in NSPS OOOO, OOOOa, 
OOOOb, and EG OOOOc based on a change in policy direction, concerns 
with the authority of the program, and a reassessment of the Program's 
expected effectiveness in light of new information.

 Revising several aspects of NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc based 
on petitions received on the March 2024 Final Rule. Specifically, the 
EPA proposes changes to the March 2024 Final Rule requirements to 
address certain petitioner concerns for liquids unloading, process 
controllers, pumps, fugitive emissions, storage vessels, covers and 
CVSs, and equipment leaks at gas plants.

 Revising the March 2024 Final Rule requirements related to 
control devices, such as requirements for continuous burning pilot 
flames, flame monitoring data deviations, control device alerts, 
visible emissions test conditions for fugitive emissions, control 
devices used on a temporary or backup basis, temporary process 
controllers, and control device categories.

 Proposing changes related to requirements for controlling 
emissions from associated gas from wells producing primarily oil. The 
EPA is proposing that routing to a sales-line is not an appropriate 
BSER for these emissions. The Agency is proposing that routing 
associated gas to a control device or a flare that achieves 95%

[[Page 68238]]

reductions in emissions or greater should be BSER instead.

 Proposing to add a new subcategory for certain well sites 
affected and designated facilities based on a variety of operational 
conditions. This aspect of the proposal also includes revisions to 
requirements that apply at certain well sites that address concerns 
related to the appropriateness of the categorization and the burden 
associated with complying with the March 2024 Final Rule requirements. 
Specifically, in this action, the EPA is co-proposing two alternative 
approaches to subcategorizing well sites:
    [ssquf] An option based on marginal and non-marginal well sites 
that would include reduced requirements for marginal wells. The EPA 
also solicits comment on an alternative approach to a marginal well 
site subcategory that would further subcategorize marginal wells based 
on production levels.
    [ssquf] An option based on conventional and non-conventional wells

D. Statutory Background and Authority

    CAA section 111 authorizes the EPA to list and regulate categories 
of stationary sources that the Administrator, ``in his judgment,'' 
finds that the source category ``causes, or contributes significantly 
to, air pollution which may reasonably be anticipated to endanger 
public health or welfare.'' \21\ The listing of a source category 
triggers an obligation to promulgate ``standards of performance'' for 
new sources and, under limited circumstances, to prescribe regulations 
under which States submit plans that establish standards of performance 
for existing sources.\22\ This provision, along with agencies' 
authority to reconsider prior regulations, provides the EPA's statutory 
authority for this proposed action.\23\

    CAA section 111(b)(1)(A) authorizes the Administrator to publish, 
and from time-to-time revise, a list of categories of stationary 
sources that the Administrator, ``in his judgment,'' finds ``causes, or 
contributes significantly to, air pollution which may reasonably be 
anticipated to endanger public health or welfare.'' Once the EPA lists 
a source category under CAA section 111(b)(1)(A), the EPA must, under 
CAA section 111(b)(1)(B), establish ``standards of performance'' for 
``new sources'' in the source category. These standards are referred to 
as NSPS. The NSPS are national requirements that apply directly to new 
sources within the relevant source category.
    Congress intended the NSPS to work together with the geography-
based national ambient air quality standards (NAAQS) program in CAA 
sections 107-110. Similar to national emission standards for hazardous 
air pollutants (NESHAPs) that limit emissions of hazardous air 
pollutants (HAPs) listed and regulated under CAA section 112, NSPS 
under CAA section 111 apply to a new source regardless of whether the 
area in which the new source is located is subject to NAAQS-related 
limitations and requirements. Accordingly, CAA section 111(a)(2) 
defines a ``new source'' as ``any stationary source, the construction 
or modification of which is commenced after the publication of 
regulations (or, if earlier, proposed regulations) prescribing a 
standard of performance under this section, which will be applicable to 
such source.'' CAA section 111(a)(4) further defines ``modification'' 
as ``any physical change in, or change in the method of operation of, a 
stationary source which increases the amount of any air pollutant 
emitted by such source or which results in the emission of any air 
pollutant not previously emitted.'' While this provision treats 
modified sources as new sources, the EPA's regulations also treat a 
source that undergoes ``reconstruction,'' by substantially replacing 
its components, as a new source.\24\

    CAA section 111(a)(1) defines ``standard of performance'' as ``a 
standard for emissions of air pollutants'' that must be promulgated or 
revised in a specified manner. When the EPA establishes or revises a 
performance standard, CAA section 111(a)(1) provides that such standard 
must ``reflect[] the degree of emission limitation achievable through 
the application of the best system of emission reduction which (taking 
into account the cost of achieving such

[[Page 68241]]

reduction and any nonair quality health and environmental impact and 
energy requirements) the Administrator determines has been adequately 
demonstrated.'' Thus, the term ``standard of performance'' as used in 
CAA section 111 makes clear that the foundation for the regulatory 
requirements for the source category is the EPA's determination of the 
BSER that is ``adequately demonstrated'' for emissions of the relevant 
air pollutants.\25\ The EPA has discretion in determining the BSER, and 
has historically followed a ``technology-based approach'' that focuses 
on ``measures that improve the pollution performance of individual 
sources,'' such as ``add-on controls.'' \26\

    To determine the BSER, the EPA first identifies the ``system[s] of 
emission reduction'' that are ``adequately demonstrated'' and then 
determines the ``best'' of those adequately demonstrated systems, 
``taking into account'' factors including ``cost,'' ``nonair quality 
health and environmental impact,'' and ``energy requirements.'' After 
determining the BSER, the EPA derives from that system an 
``achievable'' ``degree of emission limitation.'' A standard of 
performance is ``achievable'' if a technology can reasonably be 
projected to be available to an individual source at the time it is 
constructed so as to allow it to meet the standard.\27\ The EPA must 
then, under CAA section 111(b)(1)(B), promulgate ``standard[s] for 
emissions''--the NSPS--that reflect that level of stringency. The EPA 
may determine that different sets of sources have different 
characteristics relevant for determining the BSER for emissions of the 
relevant air pollutants and may subcategorize sources accordingly.\28\

    To qualify as the BSER, the system of emission reduction must be 
``adequately demonstrated'' as ``the Administrator determines.'' \29\ 
The plain text of CAA section 111(a)(1), and in particular the terms 
``adequately'' and ``the Administrator determines,'' confers upon the 
EPA the discretion to identify the appropriate system, including making 
scientific and technological determinations and considering a broad 
range of policy considerations.\30\ The D.C. Circuit has stated that 
the EPA may weigh the various factors identified in the statute and 
caselaw to determine the ``best'' system and has emphasized that the 
EPA has significant discretion in weighing the factors (cost, health 
and environmental impact, and energy requirements).\31\ The EPA has 
broad discretion in determining which adequately demonstrated system of 
emission reduction is the ``best.'' The D.C. Circuit has explained that 
``section 111(a) explicitly instructs the EPA to balance multiple 
concerns when promulgating a NSPS'' \32\ and emphasized that ``[t]he 
text gives the EPA broad discretion to weigh different factors in 
setting the standard,'' including the amount of emission reductions, 
the cost of the controls, and the nonair quality environmental impacts 
and energy requirements.\33\

    Sections III.A through III.K of this preamble present the

A. Super Emitter Program

    As part of the March 2024 Final Rule, the EPA established a novel 
form of work-practice standard and compliance assurance mechanism known 
as the Super Emitter Program, which relies on third-party entities 
certified by the Agency to detect ``very large emissions events'' \71\ 
using Agency-approved technologies and submit notifications to EPA 
personnel. The EPA transmits the third-party notification to relevant 
owners and operators, thereby triggering an obligation to investigate 
and to take any necessary corrective actions required under applicable 
standards. The EPA finalized this program as part of the 40 CFR part 60 
NSPS subparts OOOO, OOOOa, and OOOOb and as part of the presumptive 
requirements applicable to state plans under EG OOOOc, meaning that 
States are expected to establish super emitter programs analogous to 
the EPA's. Upon reconsideration, the EPA no longer believes that the 
Super Emitter Program is well-grounded in policy and law and proposes 
to rescind the third-party certification, notification, and other 
related provisions in NSPS OOOO, OOOOa, and OOOOb and EG OOOOc.

1. Background
    In the December 2022 Supplemental Proposal, the EPA sought public 
comment on a novel program intended ``to trigger swift mitigation of 
super-emitter emissions events when they are identified through 
credible information provided by regulatory authorities or approved 
qualified third-party sources.'' \72\ The EPA explained that it 
believed additional action was needed to address ``super-emitter 
emissions events'' citing one study finding ``that the top five percent 
of sources contribute over 50 percent of the total emissions'' from the 
source category, although it also acknowledged that results ``vary by

bases for the program: first, that ``super-emitters'' are ``a separate 
and distinct source of emissions'' (and therefore a ``designated 
facility''); and second, that the program ``constitutes work practice 
standards for certain sources and compliance assurance mechanisms for 
other sources.'' \75\

2. Summary of Proposed Rescission and Rationales
    The EPA is proposing to rescind the Super Emitter Program on 
several alternative policy and legal bases. First, the EPA now proposes 
that this novel program rests on insufficient evidence of the nature 
and duration of super-emitter events, defined as emissions of 100 kg/hr 
or greater, and that the same concerns that led the Agency to decline 
to treat ``super emitters'' as a distinct ``affected source'' call into 
question the

[[Page 68246]]

conceptual basis and need for the program in the first instance. 
Second, the EPA further proposes that the program is not necessary and 
provides limited additional value in light of the other requirements 
applicable to affected sources under NSPS OOOO, OOOOa, OOOOb, and EG 
OOOOc. Third, the EPA proposes that the Super Emitter Program is not 
effective and is overly broad as designed. Fourth, the EPA proposes 
that the statutory authority bases finalized in the March 2024 Final 
Rule are inadequate to maintain the program. Specifically, as explained 
below, the EPA has concerns that the program features an inappropriate 
role for third parties, does not properly function as a work practice 
standard, and does not properly function as a compliance measure.
    If finalized, the proposed rescission would remove provisions 
related to the Super Emitter Program, including for certification and 
decertification of third parties, certification and decertification of 
third-party monitoring technologies, and a source's obligations to 
respond in the event of a notification received pursuant to the Super 
Emitter Program, from 40 CFR part 60, subparts OOOO, OOOOa, OOOOb, and 
OOOOc.
    The EPA proposes that additional information and further study are 
required to evaluate the underlying premise of the Super Emitter 
Program, that is, the assertion that ``super-emitter events'' (defined 
as emissions of 100 kg/hr or greater) from a select few sources are 
responsible for the majority of source-category emissions. In the March 
2024 Final Rule, and specifically in the December 2022 Supplemental 
Proposal, the EPA believed that ``the top five percent of sources 
contribute to over 50 percent of the total emissions'' from the source 
category because of super-emitter events.\88\ For this conclusion, the 
Agency relied on a single study consisting of 2018-2020 aerial surveys 
of the New Mexico Permian Basin that acknowledged its results departed 
from those in previous studies and did not endeavor to differentiate 
among the regulatory status of emission sources or potential causes for 
the emissions. While informative, the novel analytical approach and 
results of this study had not been thoroughly vetted at the time of the 
December 2022 Supplemental Proposal, and the EPA did not revisit the 
question of the study's quality and utility in the March 2024 Final 
Rule. Indeed, the Agency acknowledged at the time that results vary by 
basin and involve a number of different potential causes and 
explanations depending on the nature and regulatory status of the 
potential source(s).\89\ At the time of the March 2024 Final Rule, the 
EPA did not have adequate information on the prevalence, nature, 
duration, and cause of large emission events, without which the program 
cannot effectively further legitimate policy ends, and thus, the EPA 
proposes to rescind the Super Emitter Program. While the Agency is 
aware of some additional information that has become available on this 
topic since the March 2024 Final Rule, the Agency proposes to conclude 
that information indicates that the Super Emitter Program is overly 
broad as designed, as explained below, which is a separate reason for 
its proposed rescission. The Agency specifically seeks comment 
providing additional studies and information bearing on super-emitter 
events and corresponding strategies to address them, including whether 
the EPA should treat them separately as a regulatory manner in the 
first instance and, if so, whether and which threshold the EPA should 
use to separately consider such events. (Question III.1a)

B. Liquids Unloading

1. Background
    Under the March 2024 Final Rule, both the NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc 
require each affected and designated gas well facility that unloads 
liquids to employ techniques (e.g., manual unloading steps taken to 
unload liquids) or technology(ies) (e.g., plunger lift systems, surface 
jet pumps, velocity strings) that minimize or eliminate venting of 
emissions during liquids unloading events. As an alternative, owners or 
operators may comply with the GHG and VOC standards by routing vented 
emissions to a control device that reduces methane and VOC emissions 
(methane only for designated facilities) from each gas well liquids 
unloading event by 95.0 percent.
    For unloading technologies or techniques that could result in 
venting to the atmosphere, the March 2024 Final Rule requires owners or 
operators to follow certain work practices. The March 2024 Final Rule 
requires that owners or operators employ and document best management 
practices to minimize venting of methane and VOC emissions for each gas 
well liquids unloading operation. Specifically, owners or operators of 
affected and designated gas well facilities that undergo liquids 
unloading events must develop, maintain, and follow a best management 
practice plan to minimize venting of methane and VOC emissions (methane 
only for designated facilities) to the maximum extent possible from 
each gas well liquids unloading operation. This best management 
practice plan must meet the following minimum criteria: (1) include 
steps that create a differential pressure to minimize the need to vent 
a well to unload liquids; (2) include steps to reduce wellbore pressure 
as much as possible prior to opening the well to the atmosphere; (3) 
unload liquids through the separator where feasible; and (4) close all 
wellhead vents to the atmosphere and return the well to production as 
soon as practicable. The standards are the same for the NSPS and the 
EG.
    Where liquids unloading events are conducted using a technology or 
technique that eliminates venting to the atmosphere, the March 2024 
Final Rule requires owners and operators to report the identification 
of the well along with the non-venting technology or technique used in 
their annual report. If more than one non-venting method is used, the 
March 2024 Final Rule requires that owners and operators maintain 
records of all the differing non-venting liquids unloading methods used 
at the well affected/designated facility.
    When unplanned venting occurs from these wells during a compliance 
period, an owner or operator is required to follow their best 
management practices plan for such events and comply with the 
associated recordkeeping and reporting requirements for those events. 
The March 2024 Final Rule requires owners and operators to maintain 
records for the number of unplanned events where emissions are vented 
to the atmosphere during a liquids unloading operation. The March 2024 
Final Rule requires owners and operators to provide the above 
recordkeeping information to the EPA in their annual report.

b. Control Device Compliance Requirements
    Background. Petitioners stated that while they generally support 
the work practice procedures finalized in 40 CFR 60.5376b, they do not 
support the covers, closed vent and control device compliance assurance 
requirements at 40 CFR 60.5376b(g), which are associated with the 
alternative compliance option of routing vented emissions to a control 
device.\119\ While the petitioners do not oppose including the 
alternative compliance option, they assert that the associated ongoing 
compliance assurance requirements are inappropriate. They explain that, 
when implementing the work practice procedures to reduce emissions from 
well liquid unloading activities as specified in 40 CFR 60.5376b(b) 
through (f), operators will review the characteristics of the well at 
the time of the event. If certain conditions (e.g., operator safety, 
equipment malfunctions) are present, an operator may need to deviate 
from a planned option for minimizing emissions and instead route gas to 
a temporary flare to minimize emissions and further reduce the amount 
of gas that would be vented by 95.0 percent. Petitioners noted that, 
given the short-term nature of liquids unloading events, the ongoing 
compliance assurance related to both a CVS and control device would be 
inappropriate since many of the activities would be forced to occur 
when liquids unloading activities are not even occurring (e.g., CVS 
inspections). They contended that it would also be untenable to 
schedule and manage these activities during unloading events given 
their variable and short duration. Petitioners recommended that the EPA 
authorize the use of a temporary flare or portable control device to 
handle emissions from liquids unloading. Specifically, they suggested 
that, due to the temporary nature of these activities, the control 
device compliance requirements should mimic those utilized for well 
completions affected facilities, i.e., a requirement to operate with a 
reliable continuous pilot flame during the liquid unloading activity. 
Petitioners noted that a temporary control device is typically used 
when the permanent control device is down for maintenance (e.g., during 
a gas plant turnaround) or to reduce emissions from intermittent 
activities (e.g., liquids unloading where feasible). In general, the 
petitioners stated that the March 2024 Final Rule does not specifically 
address temporary control devices, and as such, temporary control 
devices would presumably have to meet what they argue are untenable 
monitoring and performance testing requirements required under the rule 
for these control devices. Therefore, the petitioners urged the EPA to 
revise the March 2024 Final Rule to clearly exempt temporary control 
devices from the monitoring and performance testing requirements 
required under the rule for these control devices.

C. Process Controllers

1. Background
    Under the March 2024 Final Rule, the NSPS OOOOb final standards and 
EG OOOOc final presumptive standards contain requirements for each 
process controller affected or designated facility. These rules define 
process controller affected and designated facilities as the collection 
of natural gas-driven process controllers at a well site, centralized 
production facility, onshore natural gas processing plant, or a 
compressor station. The definitions of affected and designated 
facilities exclude natural gas-driven process controllers that function 
exclusively as emergency shutdown devices as well as process 
controllers not driven by natural gas, so neither the NSPS nor the EG 
applies to these types of controllers. The NSPS standards and the EG 
presumptive standards require process controller affected or designated 
facilities to have zero methane and VOC emissions to the atmosphere, 
except for affected or designated process controllers located in Alaska 
at a site without electrical power. For process controller affected or 
designated facilities located at Alaska sites that do not have access 
to electrical power, an owner or operator may either route process 
controller emissions through a CVS to a control device that reduces 
emissions by 95.0 percent, or they may use intermittent vent or low-
bleed process controllers (i.e., those that have a bleed rate less than 
or equal to 6 standard cubic feet per hour (scfh)) so long as they 
perform periodic monitoring of their intermittent controllers to ensure 
those controllers are not emitting to the atmosphere during idle 
periods.
    To address concerns about new sources' ability to obtain the 
equipment necessary to demonstrate compliance with the final standard 
of zero emissions immediately upon the effective date of the final 
rule, the March 2024 Final Rule NSPS allowed up to 1 year from the 
effective date of the final rule (i.e., May 7, 2025) to come into full 
compliance with the final NSPS standard of zero emissions. Until that 
date of compliance, owners and operators must demonstrate compliance 
with an interim standard which mirrored the requirements for sites in 
Alaska that do not have access to electrical power.\120\ To address 
continuing concerns about the supply chain and the ability of new 
sources to obtain the necessary equipment to comply with the process 
controller requirements by May 7, 2025, the EPA issued an IFR and 
request for comment on July 31, 2025 to revise the compliance date for 
the zero emissions standards.\121\ The EPA then responded to comments 
on the IFR and issued a final rule.\122\ The NSPS compliance date for 
the zero emissions standard for process controllers is now January 22, 
2027, and the interim standard continues to apply to process controller 
affected facilities (i.e., the same standard applicable to sites in 
Alaska without access to electricity) until that date.\123\

    Summary of Proposed Changes and Rationale. The EPA proposes to 
amend the standards for modified and reconstructed facilities under 
NSPS OOOOb and the presumptive standards in the EG OOOOc model rule for 
process controllers at compressor stations, as defined in 40 CFR

as emergency shutdown devices are not included in the affected or

here do not impact the regulatory exclusion for emergency shutdown 
devices and for controllers not driven by natural gas. The EPA proposes

modified and reconstructed sources), and new presumptive standards, for 
these high-pressure process controllers, which are based on the revised

controllers is not technically feasible or cost effective. Under the 
proposed requirements, an owner or operator may either route process 
controller emissions through a CVS to a control device that reduces 
emissions by 95.0 percent, or they may use low-bleed natural gas-
powered process controllers (i.e., those that have a natural gas bleed 
rate less than or equal to 6 scfh) in combination with intermittent 
vent process controllers so long as the owner/operator periodically 
monitors the intermittent controllers to ensure they are not emitting 
to the atmosphere during idle periods.
    The EPA considered the petitioners' concerns and the information 
provided regarding the costs and emission reductions associated with 
the process controller requirements at facilities with process 
controllers that are on high-pressure systems at transmission 
compressor stations. The EPA evaluated the data provided by the 
petitioners and contacted vendors regarding the costs of process 
controllers and actuators for high-pressure systems at these sites. The 
EPA agrees that the equipment costs are higher than those considered in 
the 2024 BSER analysis, as the Agency did not have sufficient 
information available at that time to anticipate the need for different 
process controller equipment for high-pressure systems at transmission 
compressor stations. The EPA revised the analysis performed for the 
March 2024 Final Rule on cost effectiveness of zero-emitting process 
controllers for existing, modified and reconstructed sources to include 
the new information for process controllers on high pressure systems at 
transmission compressor stations.\128\ The nature of these high 
pressure systems limits the technical feasibility of routing emissions 
from these controllers to a process, control, or sales line and also 
limits the use of self-contained process controllers. These facilities 
need to use fast-acting process controllers and actuators. Electric 
process controllers are not fast enough. Controllers driven by 
compressed air are fast enough; they are technically feasible, but 
their costs are very high. The EPA evaluated the costs and emissions 
reductions of replacing natural gas-powered process controllers with 
process controllers driven by compressed air. The EPA estimates that to 
replace natural gas-driven process controllers on high pressure systems 
with process controllers driven by compressed air at compressor 
stations, the capital costs would be $2.4 million, annualized capital 
costs would be $263,300, and emissions would be reduced by 0.2 tons per

updated values are not cost effective. Based on this determination,

determine that a different standard (and presumptive standard) for 
process controllers on high pressure systems would be warranted (a 
standard other than the zero emission standard) and evaluated other 
emissions control options. These options are explained below.

b. Modification Criteria for Process Controllers
    Background. Petitioners requested that the EPA clarify that a 
modification for process controllers occurs only when there is both an 
increase in emissions and one or more controllers are added to the 
facility. Petitioners recounted that the EPA changed the definition of 
affected facility for process controllers from a single process 
controller to the collection of all the process controllers at a well 
site in NSPS OOOOb. Petitioners also recounted that in NSPS OOOOb, the 
EPA changed the modification criteria to state, ``[f]or the purposes of 
Sec.  60.5390b, in addition to the definition in Sec.  60.14, a 
modification occurs when the number of natural gas-driven process 
controllers in the affected facility is increased by one or more.'' 
According to the petitioners, the regulatory language seems to indicate 
that process controllers would be considered modified only if there is 
an increase in emissions and the number of natural gas-driven process 
controllers is increased by one or more, but in the March 2024 Final 
Rule preamble, the EPA focused only on the number of increased 
controllers, implying that an increase in process controllers 
automatically increases emissions from the affected facility. According 
to the petitioners, there are many actions that can take place at the 
time a new controller is added to offset its emissions, such as when a 
new controller replaces an existing controller with the same or with 
higher emissions or when new controller emissions are offset by the 
removal of other controllers or adjustments in their operations. The 
petitioner reported that these concepts have long been a part of 
facility operations management to limit the need for additional 
permitting.
    Summary of Comment Solicitation. The EPA acknowledges the 
petitioners' request for clarification and is soliciting comment on 
whether revisions to the current modification determination language in 
40 CFR 60.5365b(d)(1) for process controllers are warranted. The EPA 
maintains that increasing the total number of natural gas-driven 
process controllers at a facility generally increases the emissions of 
natural gas, methane, and VOC to the atmosphere by the nature of the 
equipment, which bleeds gas continuously and/or emits gas during 
actuation events, emits gas during malfunctions of the equipment, or 
emits gas through leaks in the equipment or from connections to CVSs. 
Adding one more natural gas-emitting process controller to an existing 
set of natural gas-emitting process controllers is therefore generally 
expected to result in increased emissions. The intent and purpose of 
this provision was to simplify modification determinations by 
eliminating the need for owners/operators to determine emissions before 
and after a change in a process controller affected facility and to 
reduce the burden on permitting authorities reviewing that modification 
determination. That said, the EPA also recognizes that by statute, an 
increase in emissions is a necessary condition to a modification 
determination. The EPA also notes that the number of process 
controllers in the affected facility does

[[Page 68255]]

not increase when a new natural gas-driven process controller replaces 
an existing one, or when the addition of a process controller is offset 
by the removal of one or more existing process controllers. The 
petitioner suggests that, in some cases, operational adjustments to 
other controllers could offset the emissions of the new controller. The 
EPA is soliciting additional information on the relative change in 
emissions when these process controller replacement events occur and 
the frequency with which they occur. The EPA also requests comment on 
whether the existing modification determination language appropriately 
captures changes resulting in emissions increases, or whether 
adjustments to the current criteria are needed to reflect industry 
practices, such as clarifying what constitutes net increases in 
emissions from the source. (Question III.3d)

D. Pumps

1. Background
    Under the March 2024 Final Rule, the NSPS OOOOb final standards and 
EG OOOOc final presumptive standards contain requirements for each pump 
affected or designated facility, which is the collection of natural 
gas-driven pumps at a well site, centralized production facility, 
onshore natural gas processing plant, or compressor station. Pumps that 
are in operation less than 90 days per calendar year or that are not 
natural gas-driven are not included in the definition of affected or 
designated facility. For pump affected or designated facilities located 
at a site that has access to electrical power and for those without 
access to electrical power that have three or more natural gas-driven 
diaphragm pumps, the pump affected facility must have zero methane and 
VOC emissions to the atmosphere. For each pump affected or designated 
facility located at a site that does not have access to electrical 
power and that also has fewer than three natural gas-driven diaphragm 
pumps, emissions must be controlled if a control device is otherwise 
onsite.

summary of proposed changes, and rationale for proposed changes.
2. Additional Background and Summary of Proposed Changes and Rationale

NSPS OOOOb standards and EG OOOOc presumptive standards of zero 
emissions for existing natural gas-driven pumps that are already in 
compliance with NSPS OOOOa, which requires certain natural gas-driven 
diaphragm pumps to be routed to a control device or process that 
achieves an emissions reduction of at least 95.0 percent.\132\ 
Petitioners requested that the EPA's model rule and presumptive 
standards in EG OOOOc and the standards in OOOOb (for modified and 
reconstructed facilities) allow these existing pumps that are already 
reducing emissions by 95 percent to continue to comply with NSPS OOOOa 
instead of having to convert to the zero emissions standard (100 
percent control as opposed to 95 percent control). Petitioners implied 
that the EPA did not adequately consider the incremental cost 
effectiveness of requiring existing diaphragm pumps subject to NSPS 
OOOOa (and already achieving 95 percent control) to achieve zero 
emissions.

E. Fugitive Emissions

1. Background
    Under the March 2024 Final Rule, NSPS OOOOb includes standards for 
fugitive emissions components affected facilities and EG OOOOc includes 
presumptive standards for fugitive emissions components designated 
facilities. As described in the preamble to the March 2024 Final Rule, 
each fugitive emissions components affected facility and each fugitive 
emissions components designated facility includes the collection of 
fugitive emissions components at a well site, centralized production 
facility, or a compressor station.\135\ As defined at 40 CFR 60.5430b 
and 60.5430c, fugitive emissions include an indication of emissions 
observed from a fugitive emissions component using audible, visual, and 
olfactory (AVO), an indication of visible emissions observed from a 
fugitive emissions component using an OGI instrument, or an instrument 
reading of 500 parts per million by volume (ppmv) or greater from a 
fugitive emissions component using EPA Method 21 of appendix A-7 to 40 
CFR part 60 (EPA Method 21). 40 CFR 60.5430b defines a fugitive 
emissions component as any component that has the potential to emit 
fugitive emissions of methane or VOCs at a well site, centralized 
production facility, or compressor station. These devices include 
valves (including separator dump valves), connectors, pressure relief 
devices, open-ended lines, flanges, covers and CVSs not subject to 40 
CFR 60.5411b, thief hatches or other openings on a storage vessel not 
subject to 40 CFR 60.5395b, compressors, instruments, meters, and yard 
piping. Similarly, the EG OOOOc, 40 CFR 60.5430c contains comparable 
definitions for fugitive emission components, defined as any component 
that has the potential to emit fugitive emissions of methane at a well 
site, centralized production facility, or compressor station. This 
includes but is not limited to valves (including separator dump 
valves), connectors, pressure relief devices, open-ended lines, 
flanges, covers and CVSs not subject to 40 CFR 60.5411c, thief hatches 
or other openings on a storage vessel not subject to 40 CFR 60.5396c, 
compressors, instruments, meters, and yard piping.

    For the NSPS OOOOb, owners and operators of affected facilities 
that contain fugitive emission components follow 40 CFR 60.5397b. 
Owners and operators of fugitive emission components at affected 
facilities must develop and follow the fugitive emissions monitoring 
plan for the site consistent with 40 CFR 60.5397b(b), conduct initial 
and ongoing fugitive emission monitoring surveys as provided in 40 CFR

identified as provided in 40 CFR 60.5397b(h), and follow the proper 
recordkeeping and reporting procedures as specified in 40 CFR 
60.5397b(k). In general terms, after the initial survey, this provision 
requires monitoring and repair for the five subcategories of well sites 
and compressor stations as follows:

 Single wellhead only well sites: Quarterly monitoring 
using AVO or any other detection method (e.g., EPA Method 21, etc.).

 Multi-wellhead only well sites: Semiannual OGI (or EPA 
Method 21) monitoring and quarterly monitoring using AVO or any other 
method.

 Well sites or centralized production facilities with 
specified major production and processing equipment: Quarterly OGI (or 
EPA Method 21) monitoring and bimonthly monitoring using AVO or any 
other detection method.

 Small well sites: Quarterly monitoring using AVO or any 
other detection method.

 Compressor stations: Quarterly OGI (or EPA Method 21) and 
monthly monitoring using AVO or any other detection method.
    The third subcategory includes well sites and centralized 
production facilities that have: (1) One or more controlled storage 
vessels or tank batteries; (2) one or more control devices; (3) one or 
more natural gas-driven process controllers or pumps; or (4) two or

a. Fugitive Emissions Monitoring Detection Technologies
    Background. Petitioners requested that the EPA clarify that 
operators may use AVO, OGI, and/or EPA Method 21 as part of flexible, 
fit-for-purpose fugitive emissions monitoring plans. According to 
petitioners, the March 2024 Final Rule fails to clarify whether 
facilities can use multiple monitoring technologies or whether they 
need to use a single technology or method to demonstrate compliance. 
Petitioners also requested extensions of difficult-to-monitor and 
unsafe-to-monitor provisions for fugitive emissions monitoring surveys 
conducted using EPA Method 21 to fugitive emissions monitoring surveys 
performed using AVO.
    Summary of Proposed Changes and Rationale. The EPA proposes to 
revise 40 CFR 60.5397b(c)(2) and 40 CFR 60.5397c(c)(2) of the 
regulatory text in NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc to refer to ``technique(s)'' 
(rather than ``technique,'' in the singular) to clarify that owners and 
operators have the option to use multiple survey techniques to comply 
with requirements based on the appropriate component monitoring survey 
method used. The Agency notes that 40 CFR 60.5397b(c)(2) and 40 CFR 
60.5397c(c)(2) already include the phrase ``and/or'', suggesting 
multiple techniques could be used. The EPA notes that several 
individual techniques can be used to determine fugitive emissions on 
their own, so using multiple techniques together can also meet the 
requirements of these provisions, as long as that use is otherwise 
consistent with the relevant

[[Page 68260]]

regulatory requirements. As such, this proposed revision clarifies the 
EPA's original intent to allow usage of multiple monitoring methods 
rather than restrict owners and operators to a single method.
    The NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc currently include difficult-to-monitor 
and unsafe-to-monitor provisions in 40 CFR 60.5397b(g)(2) and (3), and 
in 40 CFR 60.5397c(g)(2) and (3), when facilities use EPA Method 21 to 
conduct fugitive emissions monitoring surveys. Considering the 
petitioners' request in this regard, the EPA acknowledges their concern 
that conducting AVO inspections shares similar monitoring challenges to 
conducting monitoring using EPA Method 21 in terms of potential 
difficulties or safety concerns when completing the inspection. As with 
EPA Method 21 inspections, the operator must visually see components to 
conduct an AVO inspection, and this may require the use of a lift or 
may require access to potentially unsafe locations. While the EPA 
expects fewer components would meet the definition of difficult-to-
monitor and unsafe-to-monitor during an AVO inspection given that AVO 
does not have the same direct proximity requirements as EPA Method 21, 
the EPA recognizes the petitioners' concern that AVO inspections could 
pose similar difficulty and safety issues as those encountered when 
monitoring is conducted with EPA Method 21. Thus, the EPA proposes to 
amend 40 CFR 60.5397b(g)(2) and (3) and 40 CFR 60.5397c(g)(2) and (3) 
to include difficult- and unsafe-to-monitor provisions for AVO 
inspections that parallel those in the current rules for monitoring 
with EPA Method 21. The EPA solicits comment on this proposal. 
(Question III.4a)

b. Definition of Fugitive Emissions Component
    Background. Reconsideration petitioners requested that the EPA 
revise the definition of fugitive emissions component in the NSPS OOOOb 
to include references to the relevant provisions of NSPS OOOO and NSPS 
OOOOa as it does for NSPS OOOOb, such that this definition would 
exclude covers and CVSs and thief hatches and other openings on a 
storage vessel, regulated under NSPS OOOO, NSPS OOOOa, or NSPS OOOOb, 
not just NSPS OOOOb. By way of a practical example, if the definition 
of fugitive emissions component excludes a thief hatch on an NSPS OOOOb 
applicable tank, fugitive surveys would not be required to include the 
thief hatch in the fugitive emissions survey conducted under 40 CFR 
60.5397b. In this example, the EPA notes that this suggested change 
would not leave the thief hatch unregulated (i.e., owners and operators 
would not be excluded from having to close an improperly opened thief 
hatch). In this case, the closed vent system and cover requirements of 
40 CFR 60.5416b would require inspections (and closing) of the thief 
hatch, which take place on the same schedule as inspections conducted 
for fugitives monitoring.
    Summary of Proposed Changes and Rationale. The EPA proposes to 
revise the definition of fugitive emissions component in NSPS OOOOb to 
include certain references to requirements under the NSPS OOOO and NSPS 
OOOOa, such that the fugitive emissions component definitions in NSPS 
OOOOb better align with the fugitive emissions component definition in 
NSPS OOOO and NSPS OOOOa. In particular, the proposed revisions would 
exclude thief hatches and other openings on a storage vessel, and 
covers and CVS components regulated under NSPS OOOO, NSPS OOOOa, or 
NSPS OOOOb from the definition of fugitive emissions component in NSPS 
OOOOb, not just those regulated under NSPS OOOOb.
    The definition of a fugitive emissions component in 40 CFR 60.5430b 
currently reads:

    Fugitive emissions component means any component that has the 
potential to emit fugitive emissions of methane or VOC at a well 
site, centralized production facility, or compressor station, such 
as valves (including separator dump valves), connectors, pressure 
relief devices, open-ended lines, flanges, covers and CVSs not 
subject to [section] 60.5411b, thief hatches or other openings on a 
storage vessel not subject to [section] 60.5395b, compressors, 
instruments, meters, and yard piping.

    The EPA proposes to revise the definition of a fugitive emissions 
component in 40 CFR 60.5430b to include exclusions from the definition 
for emission sources subject to other requirements under the rules, 
such that it would read as follows:

    Fugitive emissions component means any component that has the 
potential to emit fugitive emissions of methane or VOC at a well 
site, centralized production facility, or compressor station, such 
as valves (including separator dump valves), connectors, pressure 
relief devices, open-ended lines, flanges, covers and CVSs not 
subject to [sections] 60.5411, 60.5411a, or 60.5411b, thief hatches 
or other openings on a storage vessel not subject to [sections] 
60.5395, 60.5395a, or 60.5395b, compressors, instruments, meters,

    The CVS subject to 40 CFR 60.5411, 60.5411a, or 60.5411b and thief

60.5395, 60.5395a, or 60.5395b include specific monitoring requirements

centralized production facility or a well at an existing centralized

pieces of major production or processing equipment are added to the

production because these two measures are closely related. An increase 
in production at the well site is manifested as throughput increases to 
a tank battery located at a centralized production facility. Production 
and throughput can be linked using generally accepted engineering 
models such as condensate rates derived from gas throughput. Throughput 
to the tank battery is already tracked, and various methods are

    In developing these proposed modification criteria, the EPA 
reviewed how the Agency has previously addressed emissions increases 
related to production increases (manifested as throughput increases at 
tank batteries) in midstream operations that receive gas or liquids 
from other operations not owned or operated by the same entity, such as 
tank batteries at compressor stations. The EPA believes that 
examination of this information is relevant for modifications at 
centralized production facilities for the purposes of fugitive 
emissions components because the issues are similar: an operation 
receives liquids from other operations beyond their control. In the 
September 2020 Final Rule, the EPA explained its rationale for why 
different applicability criteria were appropriate for tank batteries in 
the midstream operations that are designed to receive liquids from 
multiple well sites over a longer period of time.\158\ The EPA carried 
this rationale forward in the March 2024 Final Rule, for tank batteries 
located in the midstream operations, to require operators of those 
tanks to determine the potential for emissions using throughput 
established in a LPE permit or the projected maximum average daily 
throughput.\159\ Similarly, in the March 2024 Final Rule, the EPA 
finalized separate modification criteria for existing tank batteries 
located in the midstream operations at 40 CFR 60.5365b(e)(3)(ii)(D) 
which allows the increase in throughput to be compared to the same LPE 
limit on throughput or the projected maximum average daily throughput 
used in 40 CFR 60.5365b(e)(2)(iii). The EPA stated that such provisions 
should address the receipt of liquids from upstream production 
facilities owned by third parties.\160\ The EPA now understands from 
the petitioners that, similar to compressor stations, centralized 
production facilities often are ``overbuilt'' to accommodate future 
production received from multiple well sites, and that while they can 
typically accommodate increases in throughput up to forecasted 
production used in the design, in some instances they are not in 
control of the offsite actions which increase that throughput. For this 
reason, the EPA now believes that the same rationale as the EPA used 
for midstream tank batteries also applies to tank batteries at 
centralized production facilities, which base their design on planned 
growth coming online over time to account for future growth, often 
beyond their control. Thus, for throughput changes brought on by 
actions (e.g., drilling a new well or fracturing or refracturing a 
well) at offsite well sites feeding the centralized production 
facility, while the EPA previously thought that tracking those actions 
at the offsite wells would be a straightforward method to determine if 
production to the centralized production facility increased (without 
tracking throughput), the EPA now proposes that a more appropriate 
approach is to determine whether a production increase would result in 
an increase in emissions above the previously estimated emissions based 
on throughput increases beyond design capacity.

production facility's design capacity appropriately captures emissions 
increases resulting from production-related changes in the method of 
operation of the stationary source, consistent with the definition of

can be accommodated under the permitted or design capacity to 
constitute a change in the method of operation. Thus, the Agency is 
proposing that such increases would not trigger a modification, as that 
term is defined under CAA section 111(a)(4), unless accompanied by a 
physical change, such as adding a tank, adding additional major 
production equipment, or otherwise increasing capacity.\162\

    Fourth, there also are potential ``hardware'' changes at the 
centralized production facility that the EPA proposes to reflect in the 
modification criteria because they could result in an increase in 
fugitive emissions. These include the replacement or modification of 
one or more storage vessels such that the cumulative storage capacity 
is increased, as these changes could increase throughput beyond design 
capacity and thus would be considered modifications for the same 
reasons as discussed above. Other hardware changes that result in 
additional fugitive emissions include the addition of one or more 
pieces of ``major production and processing equipment'' (with attendant 
additional fugitive emissions components). Because emissions increases 
are associated with the addition of fugitive emissions components, the 
Agency is proposing that they would be considered modifications, even 
if they are not associated with an increase in throughput above design 
capacity. Further, the EPA recognizes that the addition of a new onsite 
well (with attendant fugitive emissions components) or the fracturing 
or refracturing of onsite wells are within the control of the operator 
of the centralized production facility and may also result in the 
addition of fugitive emissions components and thus lead to emissions 
increases. Accordingly, these are included in the proposed modification 
criteria as well.
    The EPA believes that the proposed revisions to the modification 
provisions would continue to capture all instances in which emissions 
at a centralized production facility increase. However, these revisions 
would base that determination on actions occurring at the centralized 
production facility itself. The EPA believes that the proposed 
revisions would appropriately focus the modification criteria on 
actions under the control of, or within the knowledge of, the operator 
of the centralized production facility rather than on actions occurring 
at offsite wells for which the operator may not have control or 
knowledge. The proposed changes are still expected to appropriately 
identify when there is an increase in VOC and methane emissions a) 
based on an increase in volumetric throughput above the design capacity 
to the centralized production facility; or b) when there are additional 
fugitive emissions components added, but the proposed changes do focus 
on information known by or actions under control of the centralized 
production facility.

F. Storage Vessels

1. Background
    NSPS OOOOb contains requirements for a storage vessel affected 
facility, defined as a tank battery that has the potential for VOC 
emissions equal to or greater than 6 tpy or methane emissions equal to 
or greater than 20 tpy. The 20 tpy methane threshold for applicability 
also applies to a tank battery under the EG OOOOc. A tank battery, 
according to at 40 CFR 60.5430b and 60.5430c, is ``a group of all 
storage vessels that are manifolded together for liquid transfer. A 
tank battery may consist of a single storage vessel if only one storage 
vessel is present.'' Storage vessel affected facilities under NSPS 
OOOOb and designated facilities under EG OOOOc must determine their 
applicability (i.e., the potential for VOC or methane emissions) and 
may include LPE limits in the determination. When determining the 
potential for VOC or methane emissions, operators of storage vessels 
not subject to LPE limits may exclude any vapor from that storage 
vessel which is recovered and routed to a process through a vapor 
recovery unit (VRU) operated in accordance with the cover and CVS 
requirements.
    Under the March 2024 Final Rule, the applicability thresholds for 
tank batteries located at well sites and centralized production 
facilities are determined within 30 days of startup of production, or 
within 30 days after one of the actions described below relating to 
modifications. The applicability thresholds for tank batteries not 
located at a well site or centralized production facility (e.g., tank 
batteries at onshore natural gas processing plants) are determined 
prior to startup, or within 30 days of one of the actions described 
below relating to modifications, using throughput as determined by an 
LPE limit on throughput or the projected maximum average daily 
throughput.\167\ The March 2024 Final Rule also established 
``modification'' criteria to determine when an existing tank battery 
becomes subject to NSPS OOOOb. Under the March 2024 Final Rule, a 
``modification'' of a tank battery occurs when: (1) a storage vessel is 
added to an existing tank battery; (2) one or more storage vessels are 
replaced such that the cumulative storage capacity of the existing tank 
battery increases; or (3) throughput to the tank battery increases, and 
the potential for VOC or methane emissions meets or exceeds the 
applicability thresholds of 6 tpy VOC or 20 tpy methane, 
respectively.\168\

 Recordkeeping by the owner or operator that demonstrates

 Periodic reporting that demonstrates continuous

G. Covers and CVSs

1. Background
    Under the March 2024 Final Rule, the NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc final 
standards include requirements for CVSs. CVSs route emissions from 
wells (i.e., oil wells when routing associated gas to a control 
device), process controllers, pumps, centrifugal compressors, 
reciprocating compressors, and storage vessel affected and designated 
facilities to a control device or to a process. In addition, NSPS OOOOb 
and EG OOOOc include cover requirements to ensure compliance with the 
standards for centrifugal compressors, reciprocating compressors, and 
storage vessel affected and designated facilities.
    Under the March 2024 Final Rule, each CVS must be designed and 
operated to capture and route all gases, vapors, and fumes to a process 
or to a control device and comply with an emissions limit of no 
identifiable emissions (NIE). NIE ``means, for the purposes of covers, 
CVSs, and self-contained natural gas-driven process controllers and as 
determined according to the provisions of 40 CFR 60.5416b,\185\ that no 
emissions are detected by AVO means when inspections are conducted by 
AVO; no emissions are imaged with an OGI camera when inspections are 
conducted with OGI; and equipment is operating with an instrument 
reading of less than 500 ppmv above background, as determined by EPA 
Method 21 of appendix A-7 to this part when inspections are conducted 
with EPA Method 21.'' \186\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \185\ The cite is 40 CFR 60.5416c for EG OOOOc.
    \186\ See 40 CFR 60.5430b and 60.5430c.

    Covers must form a continuous impermeable barrier over the entire 
surface area of the liquid in the storage vessel, over the centrifugal 
compressor wet seal fluid degassing system, or over the reciprocating 
compressor rod packing emissions collection system. Each cover opening 
must be secured in a closed, sealed position (e.g., covered by a 
gasketed lid or cap) whenever material is in the unit on which the 
cover is installed, except during those times when it is necessary to 
use an opening, such as to inspect equipment or to remove material from 
the equipment.
    The March 2024 Final Rule also includes initial and continuous 
compliance requirements with the NIE requirement through OGI or EPA 
Method 21 monitoring and AVO inspections conducted at the same 
frequency as the fugitives emissions monitoring for the type of site 
where the CVS and cover are located.\187\ The EPA stated in the March 
2024 Final Rule that emissions detected by AVO, OGI, or EPA Method 21 
constitute a deviation of the NIE requirement until a subsequent 
inspection determines that the CVS and cover operate with NIE.\188\ The 
EPA also discussed, in the December 2022 Proposed Rule, that ``[a]ny 
identified emissions would be a violation of this [NIE] emissions limit 
. . .'' \189\ Each CVS requires inspection to ensure that the CVS 
operates with NIE initially within 30 calendar days after startup of

provisions. Petitioners also stated that the EPA previously rejected 
the applicability of numeric emissions limitations to fugitive 
emissions components. Petitioners noted comments made on the December 
2022 proposed rule arguing that the requirement to operate with NIE 
applies as a work practice standard. Petitioners asserted that they 
also raised concerns with the NIE requirement in the rulemaking process 
and contended that the EPA declined to address these concerns and did 
not discuss the consequences of imposing what they allege is a 
technically infeasible requirement. Petitioners asserted that the EPA's

requirement is contrary to determining the BSER because no single

    Summary of Proposed Changes and Rationale. The EPA now recognizes 
that even under the best scenarios, components on the CVS and cover are 
subject to wear and tear, and that some emissions may be beyond the 
control of the operator. The Agency therefore proposes that such 
emissions are addressed through routine monitoring and repair 
requirements, and that a detection of emissions does not constitute an 
immediate deviation, but the source instead will have the opportunity 
to repair.\196\ For these reasons, the EPA believes that changes to the 
March 2024 Final Rule's requirements for covers and CVS can be made 
that would maintain robust design requirements, while allowing for 
flexibility in repairing emissions and defects related to normal wear 
and tear, without subjecting the source to immediate non-compliance.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \196\ The requirement to record and report defects and emissions 
still would apply as well as the requirement to report and record 
each defect or emissions identified during each inspection and the 
date of repair or the date of anticipated repair if the repair is 
delayed.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The EPA proposes changes to 40 CFR 60.5411b and 60.5411c to create 
two-fold design and operational requirements for covers and CVSs. The 
first part of the requirement is the design requirement. The EPA 
proposes to remove the requirement at 40 CFR 60.5411b(a)(3) and (b)(4) 
and 60.5411c(a)(3) and (b)(4) that CVSs and covers are designed with 
NIE. The EPA proposes no changes to any other design requirements in 40 
CFR 60.5411b and 40 CFR 60.5411c. Specifically, for CVSs, these design 
requirements that the EPA is not proposing to remove require per 40 CFR 
60.5411b(c) and 60.5411c(c) that the CVS be ``of sufficient design and 
capacity to ensure that all gases, vapors, and fumes from the affected 
facility are routed to the control device or process and that the 
control device or process is of sufficient design and capacity to 
accommodate all emissions from the affected facility'' and require that 
a design certification is submitted. Similarly, for covers, the design 
requirements that the EPA is not proposing to remove are the 
requirements at 40 CFR 50.5411b(b)(1) and 60.5411c(b)(1) that the 
``cover and all openings on the cover (e.g., access hatches, sampling 
ports, pressure relief devices and gauge wells) shall form a continuous 
impermeable barrier over the entire surface area of the liquid,'' the 
requirement at 40 CFR 60.5411b(b)(2) and 60.5411c(b)(2) that ``each 
cover opening shall be secured in a closed, sealed position (e.g., 
covered by a gasketed lid or cap) whenever material is in the unit on 
which the cover is installed'' (with some operational exceptions), and 
the requirement at 40 CFR 60.5411b(b)(3) and 60.5411c(b)(3) that 
``storage vessel thief hatch shall be equipped, maintained and operated 
with a weighted mechanism or equivalent, to ensure that the lid remains 
properly seated and sealed under normal operating conditions''.
    The second part of the current regulatory standard includes the 
requirement to operate the CVS and cover with NIE. The EPA proposes no 
changes to this operational requirement in 40 CFR 60.5411b(a)(3) or 
60.5411c(a)(3) and 60.5411b(b)(4) or 60.5411c(b)(4), for CVS and covers 
under NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc, respectively. The EPA does, however, 
propose changes to the initial and continuous cover and CVS inspection 
and monitoring requirements at 40 CFR 60.5416b and 60.5416c. First, the 
EPA proposes to add the phrase ``and repair'' to the inspection 
procedures of 40 CFR 60.5416b(a) and 60.5416c(a) in order to specify 
that the design and operational requirements are met through both 
inspections and repairs. In this same Preamble section, the EPA 
proposes to specify that the inspections and repair procedures are used 
to demonstrate compliance with both design and operational requirements 
for the CVS or cover (changed from demonstrating that the CVS or cover 
operates with NIE).
    The EPA also proposes changes to the NIE test methods and 
procedures in section 40 CFR 60.5416b(b) and 60.5416c(b). First, the 
EPA proposes new criteria which demonstrate compliance with the 
operational NIE requirements. Through these revisions, the EPA proposes 
that NIE would mean operating with no emissions or defects, or when 
emissions or defects are found, facilities make repairs within the 
required timeframes or meet the delay of repair provisions when 
applicable. Next, in the repair provisions of 40 CFR 60.5416b(b)(5) and 
60.5416c(b)(5), the EPA proposes a timeframe for repair of 24 hours, 
without an option for delay of repair. If a source cannot repair the 
emissions or defect within 24 hours, to avoid recording such emissions 
as deviations, they must make repairs as soon as practicable, which 
includes making a first attempt at repair no later than 5 days of 
detecting the emissions or defect and the final repair made within 30 
days of detecting the emissions or defect, or they may put the source 
of emissions or defect on delay of repair, if the conditions for delay 
of repair (e.g., repair is technically infeasible without a shutdown) 
are met. While the longer timeline for repair is a pathway to 
compliance with the operational NIE requirement, the EPA proposes to 
alter its position stated in the preamble of the March 2024 Final Rule 
that ``any identified emissions would be a deviation of this emissions 
limitation'' and proposes that a deviation of the design requirement 
would occur when emissions or defects are found, and the repairs are 
not made in the 24-hour timeframe.
    For chronic leaks occurring during a year on the CVS or cover, the 
EPA proposes an investigative analysis. The EPA proposes that after the 
third emissions event in a year from the CVS or cover, an investigative 
analysis must be conducted within 10 days after the third emissions 
event or defect to determine if operation, maintenance, failure to 
repair, or design cause(s) caused the emissions event or defect. If the 
emissions event or defect is determined to be due to design cause(s), 
the EPA proposes that such situation constitutes a deviation of the 
design requirements for CVSs and covers. If the emissions or defect is 
determined to be due to a failure to adequately repair the source of 
the emissions or defect during the prior repair attempts, the EPA 
proposes that this situation constitutes a deviation of the repair 
requirements. If the facility determines emissions or defects are 
caused by operation, maintenance, or other cause(s), this situation 
constitutes a deviation of the operational requirements of the CVS or 
cover. The EPA proposes that the facility must determine the number of 
emissions or defects detected in a year on a rolling quarterly basis

    The EPA proposes not to change the ``no detectable emissions'' 
requirement for pumps and valves complying with the alternative 
standards for process unit equipment affected facilities. The following 
paragraphs discuss the rationale for the proposed changes relating to 
NIE for CVSs, covers, and self-contained pneumatic controllers.
    The EPA carefully considered the petitioners' concerns regarding 
emissions and defects from CVSs, covers, and process controllers and 
re-evaluated those requirements in the March 2024 Final Rule. The 
provisions for the CVS and cover intend for the control device (or 
process) to capture and route emissions generated at the emissions 
source, such as a storage vessel or compressor, thereby ensuring 
achievement of the underlying standard of performance for the emissions 
source. The EPA has seen, through implementation of the NSPS, that 
inadequate sizing of the CVS and cover (notably on storage vessels 
subject to the March 2024 Final rule) can result in the inability to 
accommodate all emissions, leading to over-pressurization events. An 
example includes liquid flowing from a separator to the storage 
vessel.\198\ These over-pressurization events can result in actuations 
of pressure-relief devices which route emissions directly to the 
atmosphere. In this way, the pressure-relief device routes only some 
emissions to the control device, so the facility fails to meet the 
underlying emissions standard. Therefore, the EPA continues to believe 
that CVS and covers must meet robust design requirements, ensured by 
adequate ongoing monitoring.

    As discussed previously, after reviewing the comments and examples 
provided by the petitioners, the EPA believes that even under the best 
scenarios, components on the CVS and cover may have wear and tear from 
the environment and emissions may often be beyond the control of the 
operator, making them similar to other fugitive emissions sources which 
allow for routine monitoring and repair without

[[Page 68272]]

subjecting a source to an immediate deviation when emissions are 
detected. Similarly, even with properly designed gasket materials, 
which include weighted mechanisms and withstand weather conditions and 
exposure to the composition of the fluid in the storage vessel, dirt 
and debris can affect the seating and seal of covers such that 
emissions may occur. The EPA also supports new detection methodologies 
and voluntary emissions detection efforts and recognizes that a NIE 
requirement which subjects a source to immediate violations from the 
detection of emissions may be counter to the Agency's goals of 
incentivizing the use of advanced technology. For these reasons, the 
EPA believes that making changes to the March 2024 Final Rule's 
requirements would still enable owners, operators, and the Agency to 
identify design flaws in covers and CVSs while allowing for flexibility 
in repairing emissions and defects related to normal wear and tear 
without subjecting the source to immediate non-compliance.
    To accommodate these changes, the EPA re-evaluated the current 
criteria in the March 2024 Final Rule, which requires that the source 
``design and operate'' the CVS or cover with NIE (as determined by OGI, 
AVO, or EPA Method 21).\199\ The current provisions at 40 CFR 60.5411b 
and 60.5411c also require that the CVS capture and route all emissions 
to the control device (or process, when applicable) and for the cover 
to form a continuous impermeable barrier over the entire surface, with 
all openings closed except for certain process purposes. As discussed 
previously, the EPA proposes no changes to these design criteria. 
However, in enabling a leak detection and repair paradigm for emissions 
and defects related to normal wear and tear, the current criteria at 40 
CFR 60.5411b(a)(3) and (b)(4) and 60.5411c(a)(3) and (b)(4) to design 
with NIE may appear to conflict. That is, a design requirement ``to 
capture all emissions'' (emphasis added) is not the same as a design 
requirement which allows for leaks to occur (even if repairs are made). 
Accordingly, the EPA proposes to delete the requirement that the CVS 
and cover be ``designed'' to operate with NIE. In doing so, the EPA 
proposes a clear design requirement and a clear operational 
requirement. However, these requirements are not entirely independent 
of one another because--like with all monitoring--leak detection 
inspections provide evidence of the underlying performance of a system. 
Similarly, in this case, the design of the CVS or cover impacts its 
proper operation. Therefore, the design and operational requirements 
are linked for compliance and enforcement purposes. To address this 
interplay, the EPA proposes changes to the ``no identifiable emissions 
test methods and procedures'' in 40 CFR 60.5416b and 60.5416c to 
establish how the inspection and repair program ensures continuous 
compliance with both the design requirement and the operational 
requirement.

    The second proposed change to the current provisions recognizes 
that in addition to requirements to design the CVS and cover to capture 
and route all emissions to the control device, there is an ongoing 
operational requirement to operate with NIE. Compliance with the 
operational requirement includes a proposed leak detection and repair 
program. While the 24-hour repair timeline also applies, sources may 
also demonstrate compliance with the operational requirement by making 
repairs on a longer timeframe. For the reasons discussed above, the EPA 
believes that defects which require longer than 24 hours to repair 
indicate a design flaw. However, the EPA still believes there should 
still be a pathway towards compliance for the operational requirements. 
Therefore, a source which cannot repair within 24 hours may still make 
repairs under the current timeline of ``as soon as practicable,'' but 
no later than 5 days for the first attempt at repair and 30 days for 
the final repair (counted from the detection of the emissions or 
defect). Sources which comply with these operational requirement 
timelines may also place equipment on delay of repair (DOR) for valid 
reasons, as currently provided in the rule. Therefore, the EPA is not 
proposing to change the current DOR provisions for the 5/30 day repair 
timelines. As discussed previously, the EPA proposes that a deviation 
of the design requirement occurs when a facility detects emissions and 
cannot complete repair in a quick and timely (i.e., 24 hours) manner. 
The EPA proposes that deviations of the requirement to operate with NIE 
occur when a facility detects emissions using the selected method, but 
repairs fail to occur within 5/30 days and the DOR provisions do not 
apply.

which cannot be made in 24 hours, the EPA proposes an investigative 
analysis for chronic leakers to further synchronize the design and 
operational requirements. The EPA believes that continued detection of 
emissions or defects from the same CVS or cover indicates failures of 
the system due to design, operation, maintenance, failure to adequately 
repair, or other causes. For this reason, the EPA proposes that after 
the same CVS or cover experiences emissions or defects three or more 
times in a rolling calendar year, the facility must perform an 
investigative analysis. The EPA proposes this threshold because it 
represents a reasonable indicator that an underlying design,

emission occurrence may signal
